articles.title: A California home hid a covered miniature town and working model railway in its backyard; the 1,460-sq-ft pool property listed at $425,000 and sold in February for $415,000
articles.summary: A modest single-family home in East Hemet, California, carried a surprise that most buyers would never expect from the street.
articles.body: A modest single-family home in East Hemet, California, carried a surprise that most buyers would never expect from the street. Behind the three-bedroom, two-bath house sat a fully built, covered miniature town complete with a functioning model train set, all tucked into a backyard that also includes an in-ground pool and an above-ground spa. The 1,460-square-foot property listed in December 2025 for $425,000 and sold on February 27, 2026, for $415,000, according to Zillow and Realtor.com.A pool home with a hidden railway cityThe house at 41011 Stetson Avenue sits on a corner lot in East Hemet, a community in Riverside County about 90 miles southeast of Los Angeles. Built in 1971, the home offers three bedrooms, two bathrooms and a circular front driveway with dual street access, providing extra parking space for vehicles or recreational toys. Inside, the primary suite features a private bath and French doors that open to the covered patio and backyard. The backyard is described in listings as a true oasis, with a gunite in-ground pool, an expansive concrete deck for lounging and entertaining, and charming storage sheds designed to resemble an Old West ghost town. Solar panels, leased at the time of sale, help offset energy costs.An above-ground spa adds to the relaxation options, making the outdoor space suitable for both summer days and cooler evenings, as per the reports.The standout feature, however, is the backyard model train city.Listings include a fully constructed, covered miniature town with a working model train set, offering a unique mix of charm, creativity and resort-style living. For model railroad enthusiasts, the setup is more than just a hobby, it’s a custom-built environment that can be enjoyed year-round under cover. A backyard experience like no other Model railroads are often kept in garages, basements or dedicated rooms, but this property takes the concept outdoors on a bigger scale. The covered miniature town protects the layout from sun and rain while still being part of the backyard experience.Owners and guests can enjoy the pool and patio area while watching trains run through a detailed streetscape of buildings, bridges and scenery.The Old West theme of the storage sheds complements the railway city, creating a cohesive aesthetic across the backyard. Ghost-town-style structures can serve both as storage and as part of the overall scene, blending practical use with visual appeal.For families and hobbyists, the setup offers a rare combination of recreation, entertainment and creative expression in a single outdoor space.Such a feature is uncommon in the typical pool-home market. Most listings emphasise square footage, number of bedrooms, lot size and standard amenities like pools and spas. A working model railway city adds a layer of personality and niche appeal that can attract a specific type of buyer, one who values the opportunity to continue or expand an existing layout rather than starting from scratch.Pricing and sale in the East Hemet marketThe home was listed for $425,000 in December 2025, with a price per square foot of about $291. At 1,460 square feet on an 8,712-square-foot lot, the property falls within the mid-range for single-family homes in East Hemet. The median listing price for homes with pools in Hemet has hovered around $425,000 in recent market snapshots, placing this home in line with local expectations for a pool property, reported Compass.The home sold for $415,000 on February 27, 2026, just under its original list price. In early 2026, the median price for homes sold in East Hemet was about $416,000, according to data from Realtor.com.That suggests the final sale price was broadly in line with the local market, even with the unusual backyard feature.For the buyer, the purchase includes not only a move-in-ready pool home but also a custom model-railway installation that would be costly and time-consuming to replicate. For the seller, the sale demonstrates that highly personalised features can find a market, even if they appeal to a narrower pool of buyers. The key is pricing the home appropriately and allowing enough time for the right buyer to appear.Why such properties can be hard to valueHomes with specialized improvements such as a covered miniature town and working railroad can be difficult to value using standard comparables. Appraisers and agents tend to look at similar properties in terms of size, age, location and standard amenities such as pools, garages and upgrades. A model railroad city does not fit neatly into those categories, and its value may depend heavily on how much a given buyer wants it. Some buyers may see the railroad as a liability, worrying about maintenance, power use or the effort needed to keep the layout in good condition. For some, it’s a major asset, seeing the time, skill and money that has gone into building a detailed, covered town with a working train set.That variation in perception can impact how quickly the house sells and how close the final sale price comes to the original list price. In this case, the home sold for $10,000 below list, a modest discount in a market where many properties see similar or larger adjustments. The presence of the pool, solar panels and corner-lot location likely supported the base value, while the railway city added a unique selling point that helped the property stand out in listings.A niche feature in a mainstream marketThe Stetson Avenue property illustrates how a highly specialised feature can coexist with more conventional real estate attributes. The house itself is a straightforward three-bedroom, two-bath pool home, the kind that appears regularly in Hemet listings. The miniature town and model railway transform it from a standard property into a conversation piece that appeals to hobbyists and creative buyers. For model-railway clubs and enthusiasts, such a setup is rare in a residential backyard. Most layouts are indoors, limiting the sense of being outside while operating the trains. A covered outdoor city allows operators to enjoy fresh air and garden surroundings while running trains through a detailed environment, something that indoor layouts cannot fully replicate. The sale also shows that unique homes can find buyers without needing to strip out the very features that make them different. Rather than removing the railway city to appeal to the broadest possible market, the sellers kept it intact and let the property speak to the right audience. articles.title: CPT restriction for international students: Universities challenge new ICE policy, says it was announced abruptly
articles.summary: International students in the US were suddenly told by their colleges in August that they would no longer be allowed to do Curricular Practical Training
articles.body: International students in the US were suddenly told by their colleges in August that they would no longer be allowed to do Curricular Practical Training as the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sent messages to colleges that if practical training is a must for the course, then American students should also do it -- otherwise there should be no room for practical training only for international students. Colleges and universities issued notices immediately to this effect which practically stopped CPT.Now, the Association of American Universities, Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts challenged the ICE memo and said colleges and universities were not given adequate time to respond.Abrupt changes; international students come to US for internshipsPrompted by the ICE memos, colleges and universities across the US paused or halted CPT authorizations. The lawsuit said that CPT has been a hallmark of US education, as it offers hands-on training to international students. “Changing how CPT is administered through broadcast messages, without formal rulemaking, is an aberration that must be challenged,” said NAFSA Executive Director and CEO Fanta Aw. “These abrupt changes have placed Designated School Officials—the professionals responsible for advising international students and ensuring institutional compliance—in an untenable position, forcing them to navigate significant new restrictions and uncertainty without the clarity and due process that formal rulemaking provides. Hands-on, experiential learning is a hallmark of a U.S. education, and restricting access to it in this way is already disrupting opportunities for international students. The consequences extend well beyond individual students and campuses. Driving away international student talent will have long-term consequences for U.S. research, innovation, workforce development, and global competitiveness.”Here's what happened to CPT in August 2026CPT is an internship program only for F-1 students. Unlike OPT, CPT is authorized by the school's DSO (Designated School Official) in SEVIS (Student and Exchange Visitor Information System) and does not require an Employment Authorization Document from USCIS. The administration saw this as a backdoor for F-1 students to gain entry to the job market.On August 12, ICE said that CPTs could be authorized only if the training is integral ro the course and in that case, all students should do that -- not only international students.On August 24, another message followed that said CPT can't be optional. If it's optional, then there is already a program for it -- OPT.Only a lawsuit has been filed and no order has been passed. But the outcome will decide whether elective, for-credit internships reemain available to international students.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Meet Jameson Mallon-Echols, South Dakota engineering student who pulled a trapped teen from a burning car;  now Rapid City has honoured the football captain with an Act of Heroism Award
articles.summary: Sometimes courage arrives before there is time to think about it.
articles.body: Sometimes courage arrives before there is time to think about it. For Jameson Mallon-Echols, a routine drive in Houston turned into a life-or-death rescue when he watched a car lose control, cross the median and crash. According to a report by KOTA Territory, Mallon-Echols, a junior mechanical engineering student at South Dakota Mines and captain of its football team, was driving to a friend's house on June 11 when he witnessed the accident. He immediately pulled over, called 911 and ran towards the wreck. As per the report, three teenagers were inside the vehicle, including the 16-year-old driver, who was seriously injured and trapped, while the two other passengers needed help getting out. Scroll down to read this story of bravery.Into the burning carAccording to the online report, Mallon-Echols first helped the two teenagers escape the vehicle before turning his attention to the driver. The situation became even more dangerous when flames began spreading underneath the driver's seat. With the teenager still trapped, Mallon-Echols used his shirt in an attempt to smother the flames. Another man at the scene managed to release the driver's seat belt, allowing the two men to concentrate on getting the injured teenager out, the report states. The rescue required more than simply pulling him free. Pieces of metal were holding the teenager inside the wreckage, and the men had to remove them before they could extract him. They eventually managed to free the teenager and carry him across the road, putting distance between him and the burning vehicle. Within moments, the car was engulfed in flames.Paramedics arrived and took the injured teenager to hospital. Mallon-Echols remained at the scene into the early hours of the morning, assisting police and answering questions about what he had witnessed, the online report adds.Honoured in Rapid CityMonths later, the rescue was recognised far from the Texas road where it happened, the latest report states. The Rapid City Common Council honoured Mallon-Echols with an Act of Heroism Award, recognising his actions during the crash. The award was presented by Ward 5 Councilwoman Laura Armstrong. The recognition also marked Mallon-Echols as the recipient of Rapid City's first Hometown Hero award, highlighting an act of courage that extended well beyond his role as a student and athlete.More than a football captainAt South Dakota Mines, Mallon-Echols is known as a football captain and mechanical engineering student. His actions in Houston, however, offered a different glimpse of the qualities he brings beyond the field. The rescue demanded quick judgment, physical effort and composure in an increasingly dangerous situation. Rather than waiting for emergency responders to arrive, he stepped towards the wreck and remained involved until the injured teenager had been taken to safety.South Dakota Mines President Brian Tande, head football coach Charlie Flohr and athletic director David Crum were among those present for the award presentation. For Rapid City, the honour was not simply about one dramatic moment. It was a recognition of the instinct to help when circumstances are frightening and uncertain.Images Courtesy: istock and KOTA TerritoryYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Two UK neighbours fought over whether a hedge boundary ran through the middle or outer edge; after losing her appeal, one must pay £108,402 upfront toward 70% of the other's costs
articles.summary: A bitter legal battle between two Torquay homeowners over a hedge boundary measurement concludes, leaving one neighbour with a staggering £108,402 bill for legal costs after losing an appeal.
articles.body: The legal dispute centred on a hedge separating two homes in Torquay, England, with a disagreement over a few millimetres of land eventually turning into a costly court battle.A homeowner who lost an appeal over the precise position of the boundary between her property and her neighbour’s has been ordered to pay £108,402 upfront towards 70% of his legal costs, as per court documents.The case involved Ms Douglas, owner of 43 Mead Road, and Mr Channon, who owns the neighbouring No. 41. Their disagreement concerned whether the boundary ran along the outer edge of a hedge or through the area where the hedge stood.Court rules on hedge boundaryThe dispute reached Plymouth County Court, where a trial was held from August 18 to 26 last year. Judge Mitchell considered evidence from surveyors, photographs and other material before determining the boundary.Mr Channon’s expert, civil engineer Mr Barber, had identified a line known as A-H-B as the boundary between the properties.Ms Douglas argued that the boundary should instead run along the hedge’s outer edge because she maintained that the hedge belonged to her property.The hedge had already been removed, making it impossible for the court to examine its exact position.The judge considered the legal principles governing boundaries formed by hedges. He found that where a hedge belongs to one property, the boundary would generally follow the outer edge of its stems or trunks, rather than the furthest point reached by its leaves.However, the judge found that the difference between that position and Mr Barber’s A-H-B line was only a matter of millimetres.He therefore applied the legal principle of de minimis, which means a difference is so small that the law treats it as insignificant, and declared A-H-B to be the boundary.Homeowner challenges the decisionMs Douglas appealed, arguing that the trial judge had identified one boundary under the applicable legal principle but then adopted a slightly different line as the property's actual boundary.Her lawyers also argued that experts should first have been required to establish the precise legal boundary. If they could not agree, they said, the court could then have considered the issue at another hearing.The Court of Appeal rejected those arguments.The appeal court noted that the trial judge had considered the expert evidence, photographs and other material and had personally visited the properties. It found that he was entitled to conclude that the difference between the competing lines was only a few millimetres.The court also rejected the argument that the ruling effectively deprived Ms Douglas of part of her property. Any difference in the amount of land involved was considered too small to have legal significance.Other claims added to the disputeThe boundary was only one part of the wider case.Ms Douglas had also brought allegations involving trespass and nuisance against Mr Channon and a previous owner. She sought damages and other remedies, including claims related to work that she said had destabilised her land.Mr Channon denied the allegations and filed counterclaims of his own. They included claims involving nuisance, trespass, alleged harassment and the value of his property.His counterclaim was worth more than £200,000, although much of it was unsuccessful.The judge also found that Ms Douglas's main claim had failed, including her allegations concerning stabilisation work.Appeal court upholds £108,402 costs orderMs Douglas argued that she should not have to pay such a large share of Mr Channon's legal expenses because she had successfully defeated most of his counterclaim.The Court of Appeal disagreed.It said judges can consider which party succeeded on the main issues, how much those issues contributed to the overall case and how the litigation was conducted. The trial judge had already taken Mr Channon's unsuccessful counterclaims into account when deciding the costs.Instead of making Ms Douglas responsible for all of Mr Channon's costs, the judge ordered her to pay 70%.The Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal, leaving both the boundary ruling and the costs order in place.Ms Douglas must therefore pay £108,402 upfront towards Mr Channon's costs, with the final amount to be determined under the 70% order.The court battle ultimately turned on a boundary difference measured in millimetres, but the wider litigation involved expert evidence, multiple claims and substantial legal costs.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kremlin backs India’s Ukraine peace push, thanks New Delhi for readiness to broker solutions
articles.summary: Russia has welcomed India’s readiness to make a “feasible contribution” towards resolving the Ukraine conflict.
articles.body: Russia has welcomed India’s readiness to make a “feasible contribution” towards resolving the Ukraine conflict. On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was grateful to New Delhi for its willingness to help and the ideas it has proposed.“Indeed, India is declaring readiness to make a feasible contribution to resolving the situation surrounding Ukraine,” Peskov said, according to state-run TASS, while responding to reports that India had sent a new three-part proposal for a peaceful resolution.“We are grateful to our Indian friends for such readiness and the ideas that are being offered,” he added.Peskov’s remarks come days after Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said India’s proposal for a possible ceasefire was the “broadest” among four offers received by Kyiv. The other proposals were from Turkiye, Egypt and the US.“We have four proposals. The broadest one is India’s proposal. We are ready for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire, but only in this combination,” Sybiha told reporters in Kyiv on Friday, according to European Pravda.India’s efforts have also received praise from Russian president Vladimir Putin.Ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi last month, Putin and Modi held talks during which the Russian leader briefed the Prime Minister on the Ukraine conflict and ongoing peace initiatives.On Friday, Putin said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had “good ideas” aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions to the conflict.“Prime Minister Narendra Modi is one of those world leaders who, despite our very good and even friendly relations, personal good relations, constantly raises the question and asks the question about putting an end to the conflict in Ukraine,” Putin said.“He has an avid interest and very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions. In that sense, naturally, the Prime Minister takes a neutral position but with an interest in the end of the conflict,” he added.Putin also said, “I think it’s my duty to say that directly. And we are thankful to the Prime Minister for his ideas.”Modi has repeatedly maintained that India is willing to support meaningful efforts towards peace. Responding to a question on India’s role, he said, “I have already indicated India’s willingness to support meaningful efforts aimed at achieving a peaceful resolution of the conflict.”External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said on Sunday that India had moved beyond advocacy and intensified engagement with both Kyiv and Moscow. He said New Delhi was focusing on issues including the safety of shipping in the Black Sea, grain exports and energy supplies.India has consistently advocated dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the conflict, now in its fifth year. Ukraine, meanwhile, has called for an unconditional ceasefire, including an end to attacks on energy and port infrastructure and a halt to hostilities in the Black Sea.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Arizona tested highways made quieter with ground-up tyres; federal researchers measured before-and-after traffic noise at roads and nearly 95 nearby homes
articles.summary: Discover how Arizona's innovative use of rubberized asphalt from recycled tires significantly lowers traffic noise on highways, benefiting both residents and the environment.
articles.body: Arizona gave millions of discarded tyres a second use when it began covering sections of its Phoenix-area freeways with rubberised asphalt. The material, made with crumb rubber from used tyres, was initially valued mainly as a way to resurface roads and recycle a difficult waste product. But the pavement also had another benefit: it could reduce the noise created when vehicle tyres travelled over the road. According to the Federal Highway Administration, Arizona and the agency launched the Quiet Pavement Pilot Program in 2003 to examine whether asphalt rubber friction courses could reduce traffic noise on busy freeways and how long the effect would last. The programme covered about 115 miles of Phoenix-area freeways and involved testing the pavement's noise performance over time.Measuring the noise before and afterArizona had been using rubberised asphalt since 1988. The material combined conventional asphalt with crumb rubber made from discarded tyres. By 2005, more than 15 million tyres had been recycled through the state's rubberised asphalt programme. The quiet-pavement project was designed to measure the change rather than simply rely on residents' impressions.Three different types of measurements were taken. The first was measuring noise at the tyre-pavement interface with a test tyre. The second type of measurement was taken at around 95 residential locations near the freeways, both before and after the rubberised asphalt was installed. The third type of measurement measured roadside sound at five sites with no nearby construction.What happened after the rubber was added?These initial findings were positive. In 2005, the FHWA found an average sound reduction of around 5 decibels in residential areas. The FHWA said the project would be monitored to see whether the sound reduction lasted through the overlay’s 10- to 12-year useful life. The long-term findings helped to give a clearer insight. A 2018 Arizona Quiet Pavement Pilot Program study, conducted after about ten years of monitoring, found an average initial sound reduction of 5.2 dBA at residential locations. When tested on-road, the average initial sound reduction was 9.1 dBA, while at the tyre-pavement interface, it was 8.7 dBA.The quieter surface did not stay as quiet over time. The long-term measurements showed an average increase of about 0.5 dB per year after the initial reduction in both the tyre-pavement and roadside measurements. Even so, the study provided evidence that the rubberised asphalt could produce a measurable noise benefit beyond the immediate period after installation.From waste tyres to quieter neighbourhoodsThe project had a further environmental component. Rather than allowing old tyres to go toward disposal, they could be converted into crumb rubber and included in the roadway surface. Millions of tyres had already been recycled in Arizona in such a manner prior to the launch of the quiet pavement initiative. The method was especially useful in Phoenix, where many freeway segments had rough concrete surfaces that generated tyre noise.However, the Arizona experiment could not show that all rubberised roads reduce noise pollution equally. Factors like types of pavements used, conditions of the pavements and traffic, among others, could play a part in determining the outcome. The FHWA also reiterated the fact that the choice of the pavement should be based on issues like safety, durability and cost rather than noise reduction alone.You use AI every day. articles.title: Howard Hughes bought 30,000 barren acres west of Las Vegas in 1952 for a reported $3 an acre; the land sat largely unused for decades before becoming the 22,500-acre Summerlin community
articles.summary: A barren stretch of land on the western edge of Las Vegas once seemed to have little immediate purpose.
articles.body: A barren stretch of land on the western edge of Las Vegas once seemed to have little immediate purpose. In 1952, Howard Hughes acquired 30,000 acres there for a reported $3 an acre, intending to use the property for his California-based business interests. The plan never happened, and the land remained largely dormant for more than three decades. According to Summerlin’s official history, the property eventually became the foundation for a master-planned community that evolved into today’s 22,500-acre Summerlin.From barren land to a long-term development planHughes acquired the land in the 1950s when the western edge of the Las Vegas Valley was still largely undeveloped. Summerlin’s history says he was considering the property as a possible relocation site for some of his California-based businesses. That relocation never took place. Instead, the 30,000-acre holding sat dormant for more than 30 years.The transformation began much later, after Hughes’ Summa Corporation, the predecessor to Howard Hughes, began looking at what could be done with the enormous tract. Rather than immediately turning it into a conventional housing development, the company assembled a team of land planners to create a broader master plan for the area.Summerlin takes shape in 1988A major turning point came in 1988, when Summa announced plans for Summerlin. The community was named after Jean Amelia Summerlin, Howard Hughes’ paternal grandmother. That same year also brought an important land exchange involving the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). Under the agreement, Summa gave up more than 5,000 acres in a land exchange with the Bureau of Land Management, helping create a buffer intended to protect the nearby Red Rock Canyon area while allowing development to move forward elsewhere.This was an important part of the project's early planning because Summerlin was being designed not simply as a collection of homes, but as a large-scale community alongside the natural landscape surrounding it.The first homes arriveThe development moved from planning to construction in 1990. Summerlin's first residential village, The Hills, began development that year. The Hills covered 394 acres and was organised around a central park, schools and residential neighbourhoods. Summerlin Parkway was also completed from Rainbow Boulevard to Town Center Drive, providing a major connection between the developing community and US 95. At the time, locals reportedly nicknamed it the “road to nowhere” because so little development surrounded it.The first family moved into Summerlin in March 1991. Cal and Maria Champlin and their children became the community's first residents, marking the beginning of what would eventually become a much larger population centre.Building more than homesAs Summerlin expanded, its development strategy went beyond residential construction. Schools, parks, medical facilities, shopping centres, religious institutions and recreational amenities were added as new villages were built. The Summerlin Library and Performing Arts Center opened in 1993, while Summerlin Hospital Medical Center followed in 1996. The community's first public high school, Palo Verde High School, opened in 1997.Golf also became part of the community's identity. TPC Summerlin opened in 1991, and in 1996 Tiger Woods won his first PGA tournament there. The scale of construction grew rapidly. By 2001, Summerlin had completed its 20,000th new home. The community also recorded 114 new-home sales in a single week, according to its official history.A growing connection to Las VegasInfrastructure played a major role in turning Summerlin from an isolated development into an integrated part of the Las Vegas Valley. Construction began in 1992 on an eight-mile section of the 215 Beltway through Summerlin. The road created another major east-west connection and helped make the community more accessible from other parts of the valley.The development continued to add commercial and entertainment destinations. Downtown Summerlin opened in 2014, creating an urban centre with retail, dining, offices and entertainment. Later additions included City National Arena, which opened in 2017 as the Vegas Golden Knights' practice facility, and Las Vegas Ballpark, which opened in 2019.Protecting open space while expandingThe relationship between development and conservation has remained part of Summerlin's history. In 2002, another land exchange between Howard Hughes and the BLM gave 1,000 acres of highlands in Summerlin's western region to the BLM. In return, Howard Hughes received roughly 1,000 acres along the community's southern edge. The exchange expanded the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area while allowing Summerlin's development to continue in areas considered more appropriate for construction.The community also developed an extensive network of parks and trails. Summerlin's official figures now list more than 300 parks and more than 200 miles of interconnected trails.From 30,000 acres to a major master-planned communityToday, Summerlin is far removed from the largely unused desert property Hughes acquired in 1952. The official Summerlin website says the master-planned community now covers 22,500 acres and is home to more than 130,000 residents. Once the master plan is completed, the population is projected to reach approximately 200,000.What began with Hughes' purchase of a vast, barren tract for a reported $3 an acre ultimately became a decades-long development project with homes, schools, parks, hospitals, businesses, golf courses, entertainment venues and a major urban centre. The transformation was not immediate. The land remained dormant for more than 30 years before plans for Summerlin were announced in 1988. From the first village in 1990 to a community of more than 130,000 residents today, the property has evolved into one of the most prominent master-planned communities in the Las Vegas Valley.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Google told to suspend work at its data centers in 'Texas of Europe', company admits 'concerns'; to advance biodiversity plans, including tree plantings
articles.summary: Google has been told to halt work on two data centers in Europe.
articles.body: ​Google has been told to halt work on two data centers in Europe. The tech giant has been ordered to suspend construction work on projects in Finland, a country increasingly known as the “Texas of Europe” for attracting large data center investments. The Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency (LVV) issued the order to Google subsidiary Tuike Finland Oy, saying work must stop until it completes environmental impact assessments.​Google acknowledged “concerns” about the work and said it fell short of its own standards. “We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance,” a Google spokesperson told CNBC, adding that the company would follow the LVV’s guidance. Google also said it is advancing biodiversity plans for the region, including tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos.​Google ordered to halt data center work​The LVV issued the notice on Tuesday, covering data center projects planned for Muhos and Kajaani. Google must halt the specified construction activities by October 23.​The suspension applies to activities including tree removal, topsoil removal, excavation, quarrying, crushing, moving soil, ditching and construction of roads and storage areas. The order does not cover planning, measurements, soil surveys or other activities with minor impacts that can be easily restored.​Tommi Muilu, head of the environmental department at the Finnish licensing and supervision authority, said the work could affect the environment before the assessment process was completed.​“In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure,” Muilu said.​Google says it will follow the guidance​Google said it had carried out nature surveys and taken steps to protect areas it considered to have high environmental value.​“We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas,” the company spokesperson said. “As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos.”​The company said it would follow the authority’s guidance as it continues work on its broader plans.​Why Finland is called the 'Texas of Europe'​Finland has emerged as an important destination for data center projects as demand for computing infrastructure rises with the growth of AI. The country offers available land and power at a time when electricity capacity is increasingly constrained in several parts of Europe.​Several data center projects with potential capacities of hundreds of megawatts have been announced in Finland, contributing to its “Texas of Europe” nickname.​Texas has become one of the major locations for AI data centers in the US, with companies including Google, Meta, Microsoft and Anthropic announcing large infrastructure projects there.​Google's $15 billion Finland investment​The suspension comes about a month after Google announced plans to invest $15 billion in Finland through 2028. The company said the investment would go towards data centers and supporting infrastructure, including energy projects.​The planned spending would represent Google's largest investment in Europe. The company has not indicated that the latest suspension changes its long-term investment plans in Finland.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Billionaire Chris Rokos gets Wiltshire Council green light for 40-acre solar farm at Savernake Estate after neighbour objections; panels to generate 794,600 kWh for 100-bedroom Tottenham House
articles.summary: Hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos has secured planning approval to build a major solar farm on his Savernake Estate in Wiltshire, overcoming objections
articles.body: Hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos has secured planning approval to build a major solar farm on his Savernake Estate in Wiltshire, overcoming objections from neighbours who warned the project could damage the historic landscape around his Grade I-listed mansion, Tottenham House.According to SWNS, representatives of Chris Rokos submitted plans to Wiltshire Council for a solar farm covering around 40 acres of his 4,500-acre Savernake Estate. The project is intended to provide Tottenham House and its surrounding buildings with a more sustainable source of electricity and water.Rokos, who founded hedge fund firm Rokos Capital Management, has been carrying out an extensive renovation of the 100-bedroom Tottenham House in Marlborough, Wiltshire.The planning documents state that the renewable energy project is designed to help secure the estate's “long term and sustainable future” by providing “a sustainable form of power and water to enable its functional operation.”Wiltshire Council has now partially discharged a planning condition relating to construction and environmental management, allowing work on the solar array itself to move forward.Neighbours raised concerns over historic landscapeThe solar farm proposal had faced opposition from several neighbours and the local parish council, despite broader support for the restoration of Tottenham House.The proposed site is located on the northern boundary of the estate and is currently used as pasture for dairy cattle and for producing silage. It is also close to a public footpath linking the hamlet of Durley with St Katharine's Church and primary school.Opponents argued that the development could have a significant impact on the historic character of the area, which lies within a protected landscape.Nearby resident Richard Frics welcomed the restoration of Tottenham House but objected specifically to the solar installation.He argued that the panels would occupy more than one hectare and would be located within an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB), as well as a Grade II* Registered Park and Garden associated with a Capability Brown landscape.Frics also raised concerns about the potential impact on the nearby Grade II* listed stable block, claiming that glare from the solar panels could significantly alter its outlook.He described the development as a threat to the “special qualities” of the heritage landscape and warned it could establish an undesirable precedent for similar planning applications.Another neighbour, Mark Colquhoun, described the wider restoration project as “an exemplary project” but called the proposed solar farm a “substantial visual and historical intrusion.”Solar panels expected to generate 794,600 kWh of electricity annuallyOnce operational, the ground-mounted solar panels are expected to generate approximately 794,600 kilowatt hours of electricity every year.Around 44% of the electricity generated is expected to be consumed on the estate, with the remaining power exported to the local electricity grid.Planning officials concluded that the benefits of the renewable energy project outweighed the potential harm to the heritage setting.The solar panels will be screened by existing woodland and additional planting intended to reduce their visibility. They will also be installed using screw piles rather than permanent concrete foundations, meaning the array could potentially be removed in the future without leaving substantial permanent structures.The land will continue to have an agricultural function, with livestock grazing able to take place around the solar panels.Tottenham House restoration forms part of wider estate developmentThe solar farm is part of a broader package of development associated with the restoration and future use of Tottenham House.The plans also include a large water storage lagoon, a new mains water connection and landscape improvements across the estate.However, while the solar array has cleared a key planning hurdle, further environmental management details still need to be approved before some of the other elements of the wider project can proceed.Tottenham House is one of Wiltshire's most significant historic properties. The Grade I-listed mansion has undergone extensive restoration after previously appearing on the Heritage at Risk register.Savernake Estate sold for £11.25 million in 2014The Savernake Estate has a history stretching back centuries and was once a Royal Hunting Forest dating to the Norman Conquest.The estate was formerly owned by the Earl of Cardigan, David Brudenell-Bruce. In 2014, he sold the 4,500-acre Savernake Estate to a developer for £11.25 million, ending around 200 years of ownership by the same family.Rokos's plans for Tottenham House and the wider estate now combine historic restoration with renewable energy infrastructure, although the solar farm's impact on the protected landscape remains a point of contention among some local residents.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1994, Louisiana tested roads paved with crumb-rubber-modified asphalt beside conventional asphalt; after 5–7 years, the rubber sections had better rut depth, fatigue cracking and IRI performance
articles.summary: Discover how Louisiana's rubberized roads, made from shredded household tires, have demonstrated superior performance in reducing fatigue cracks and providing smoother rides compared to traditional asphalt.
articles.body: In Louisiana, roads paved with crumb-rubber-modified (CRM) asphalt performed better overall than conventional sections, according to Huang et al.'s 2002 comparative study of pavement projects across the state. The rubberized sections also performed better in rut depth, fatigue cracking and the International Roughness Index (IRI), used to measure pavement smoothness. Eight CRM pavement sections at five Louisiana highway projects were examined, each using a different crumb-rubber-modified asphalt process.The evaluation comprised a combination of laboratory testing and field measurements, including visual crack inspections, roadway roughness readings and pavement structural measurements. In these pavements, the crumb rubber was sourced from scrap tires and could be incorporated into asphalt construction through a wet or dry process. In the wet process, the rubber is mixed with an asphalt binder before it is combined with aggregates, whereas in the dry process, crumb rubber is directly introduced with the aggregate and generally replaces a portion of the fine aggregate.Rubber-modified sections were compared with conventional pavementThe Louisiana project hinged on a practical question of whether asphalt containing recycled tire rubber, once exposed to actual traffic and environmental conditions, could perform just as well as conventional mixtures. Initially, laboratory results favored the conventional mixtures because they recorded higher strength characteristics than the CRM mixtures. However, the field results showed different outcomes. The CRM pavement sections, after five to seven years of traffic, had an overall better performance in rut depth, fatigue cracking and IRI measurements than their conventional sections.The laboratory evaluation used Marshall stability and flow tests, along with indirect tensile strength, strain and resilient modulus measurements. These tests were conducted on field-compacted Marshall specimens. The comparison also included pavement structure measurements obtained through the Dynaflect system and roadway core air-void analysis, while visual inspection identified cracking. Rut depth and the International Roughness Index were also used as field performance indicators, and each CRM section was compared with a conventional control section within the Louisiana projects.Instead of a single rubberized pavement design, the eight CRM sections represented different applications. Through eight different CRM processes, researchers constructed the sections or applications across five state highway projects, and each project also included a conventional asphalt control section for direct comparison. This setup allowed the researchers to compare each rubber-modified pavement section with a conventional section at the same project rather than treating all CRM sections as one uniform pavement type.The study compared wet- and dry-process CRM applications The Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development began the research in 1994 to compare the long-term performance of crumb rubber modified hot-mix asphalt (CRM HMA) with conventional hot-mix asphalt control sections. Shen and Xie reported wet- and dry-process CRM HMA performed as well as, or better than, conventional mixes in evaluated sections. Huang and colleagues' study appeared in 2002 in Transportation Research Record. For the dry process, crumb rubber was used as a substitute for a small portion of the fine aggregate, with the particles blended with the aggregates before asphalt cement was added. Under the PlusRide method described in Shen and Xie's report, CRM particles from 4.2 to 2.0 millimetres accounted for 1% to 3% of the paving mix by weight. Generic dry technology used an equivalent or slightly lower percentage of finer CRM. The researchers concluded that the CRM sections showed better overall field performance in comparison to conventional control sections despite the latter having recorded higher strength characteristics in laboratory testing.You use AI every day. articles.title: A South Dakota biofuels CEO and his family bought land near Great Bear about two years ago, then donated 20.5 acres to expand a 220-plus-acre park that now draws more than 200,000 visitors a year
articles.summary: Jeff and Tammie Broin donate 20.5 acres to expand Great Bear Recreation Park in Sioux Falls, promoting conservation and recreation for over 200,000 annual visitors.
articles.body: Jeff and Tammie Broin donated 20.5 acres of land they acquired about two years ago to the City of Sioux Falls, expanding the southern edge of Great Bear Recreation Park.Jeff Broin, founder and CEO of POET, and his wife announced the donation this week. The land will become part of Great Bear, a park covering more than 220 acres that has been a recreation and conservation destination for about 60 years and attracts more than 200,000 visitors annually.The donated land will initially remain largely undeveloped. It will provide additional conservation space while giving the city more options for future plans.Land will remain largely undevelopedThe 20.5 acres will primarily be used as natural conservation space. There are no immediate plans for new recreational facilities on the property.Future uses will be considered through the city's park master-planning process. The donation agreement also prohibits motorised traffic on the land except for maintenance.The gift supports priorities identified in Sioux Falls' Parks and Recreation System Master Plan, approved by the City Council in late 2025. Those priorities include walking and hiking trails, natural areas and wildlife habitats.“This land donation is an investment in a beloved outdoor space and strengthens Great Bear as a four-season destination,” Sioux Falls Mayor Christine Erickson said.Family previously donated $1.3 millionThe Broins have previously contributed to Sioux Falls' outdoor recreation projects.Jeff and Tammie Broin, together with the Ashby family, donated $1.3 million through the Sioux Falls Area Community Foundation. The money helped fund an additional mile of recreational trail from Lien Park near Cliff Avenue to Bahnson Avenue.The trail includes an elevated boardwalk, which the city says is the first of its kind in the Sioux Falls parks system.The longer-term goal is to extend the trail corridor along the Big Sioux River to Great Bear and eventually connect it to Veterans Parkway, subject to funding.Great Bear attracts more than 200,000 visitorsGreat Bear offers recreation throughout the year. Its winter activities include downhill skiing, a terrain park, the Kirby Family Tubing Park, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing.During warmer months, visitors use the park's trails for hiking and mountain biking.More than 200,000 people visit Great Bear each year.“Great Bear is very thankful for the Broin Family's preservation of this unique greenway in northeast Sioux Falls and the enhancement of Great Bear Recreation Park,” said Dan Grider, the park's general manager.Donation awaits city approvalThe donation still requires approval. The Sioux Falls Parks and Recreation Board will consider the gift first, followed by the City Council if the board approves it.If accepted, the 20.5 acres will become part of the city's park system.Broin founded POET and serves as its chairman and CEO. The company operates 33 facilities across eight states, with a combined annual production capacity of 3 billion gallons of biofuels and more than 14 billion pounds of co-products.He has worked in the biofuels industry for more than 35 years and is the founding chairman of Growth Energy.“Our family truly enjoys Sioux Falls and being members of this great community,” Broin said. “We think South Dakota is a unique and amazing state and Sioux Falls is a great place to live and work.”He said the family hopes the land will help create a recreational area that can be enjoyed by future generations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump as ‘orange plague’: Gold-covered naked statue of US president unveiled at European Parliament
articles.summary: A gold statue depicting US president Donald Trump naked has been unveiled at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, with Danish artist Jens
articles.body: A gold statue depicting US president Donald Trump naked has been unveiled at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, with Danish artist Jens Galschiøt naming the eight-foot installation 'The Orange Plague'.The sculpture, covered in 23-karat gold leaf, shows Trump holding a golf club and a world-shaped ball in one hand and a set of scales in the other, according to The Independent.The statue portrays Trump standing on the shoulders of a much smaller man and is labelled “The King of Injustice”. A satirical pledge inscribed on its base reads, “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back.”Galschiøt, who is known for his politically charged sculptures, described the work as a “satirical outcry” against what The Independent described as the volatility of Trump’s green and foreign policies.In a statement, the artist said, “Trump represents one of the greatest threats to the rule-based world order, democratic values, and our common effort to solving the climate crisis.”“We must address this issue and stand together against such destructive influence,” he added.The Danish artist also took to X on Wednesday to share a photograph showing miniature versions of the sculpture. “I’m still in Strassbourg where I will be handing out 10,000 versions of the Orange Plague,” Galschiøt wrote.The installation has been backed by Danish member of the European Parliament Per Clausen, who said, “If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage.”The latest sculpture is a reworking of Galschiøt’s earlier work Survival of the Fattest, which depicts a starving boy carrying an overweight woman as a metaphor for global inequality.According to CNN, members of the European Parliament can host displays on parliament grounds, subject to official approval. Rules prohibit exhibitions deemed “offensive or of an inflammatory nature” or those that “undermine the dignity of Parliament.”The Trump sculpture is scheduled to remain in Strasbourg through Thursday. According to The Independent, it is expected to appear again in November at the UN COP31 climate conference in Turkey, where Galschiøt plans to distribute 3D-printed miniature replicas to delegates.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2022, a forgotten filing cabinet inside an old North Carolina home revealed a rare 1787 Constitution copy; it later sold at auction for $9 million
articles.summary: A rare 1787 copy of the U.S. Constitution discovered in a North Carolina filing cabinet has sold for $9 million at auction, making headlines for its historic significance and connection to the state's history. Learn more about this incredible find.
articles.body: A rare 1787 copy of the U.S. Constitution that had remained inside a filing cabinet in the Hayes house in Edenton, North Carolina, for decades sold for $9 million at Brunk Auctions in Asheville on Oct. 17, 2024. Discovered in 2022, the document is one of about 100 copies produced after the Constitutional Convention and sent to the states for ratification. It is just one of the eight signed copies known to survive, and the only privately held one, while the other seven are publicly owned.According to The New York Times, Ken Farmer, an antiques appraiser, found the document in 2022 while assessing the contents of the Hayes house in Edenton. He opened a folder kept inside a dusty filing cabinet and found a sheet of paper with the signature of Charles Thomson secretary of Congress at the time, which helped identify it as an authentic official ratification copy. The auction attracted bids that mostly rose in $500,000 increments, the Associated Press reported, reaching $8.5 million before a pause, and then a final bidder offered $9 million.What made the document distinctive The document's significance came not only from its age but from what it contained beyond the printed constitutional text. The right side of the front page was occupied by the printed constitution, alongside the entire back page and part of the left side. While the center included George Washington's letter, urging ratification, and acknowledgement that some rights held by the states would have to be surrendered for the nation's long-term interests.The document's physical condition also helped preserve evidence of its history. It was creased at the center and had become yellowed, but the printed words remained legible. Handwritten notes survived in the margins, which included the words “Adopted it must be & shall be.” Its connection to Charles Thomson was particularly important because it helped Seth Kaller, a historical documents expert, determine that the sheet was an authentic version of the official ratification copy. Likely 27 copies were signed by Thomson: two for each of the 13 states, one for the Congressional archives and only eight of those signed copies are known to have survived.Furthermore, the document belonged to a specific stage in the Constitution's adoption. In 1787, after the Constitutional Convention completed the proposed framework of the U.S. government, Congress had copies distributed to the states so they could review the document and consider ratification.A paper trail tied to North Carolina history The Hayes house where the copy was found had belonged to Samuel Johnston who was the governor of North Carolina from 1787 to 1789. Johnston also presided over the state's ratifying conventions of 1788 and 1789 and later became the state's first U.S. senator, serving from 1789 to 1793.For generations, the property had remained connected to the Johnston and Wood families. Johnston settled the property in the late 18th century, and it was later given to Edward Wood in 1865. Eventually the Hayes house became part of a 1,400-acre plantation where enslaved people were held in six cottages. For more than 150 years, the Wood family kept the property before the house and 194 acres were sold to the state of North Carolina in 2022 for more than $6 million. Farmer had been hired to assess the property’s items, including objects that were not being offered for sale and the Constitution was among the materials he examined.The state later reviewed the discovery and did not deem the document to be public property. Its eventual auction price was far above the last known sale of a Constitution copy in 1891, when a similar copy sold for $400. The $9 million sale was also distinct from the $43.2 million auction record set in 2021 for another early Constitution copy, which belonged to a different group of surviving copies.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2011, Iowa built US 6’s Keg Creek bridge off-site and installed it in 16 days; the project cut total costs by $440,000
articles.summary: In 2011, Iowa's Keg Creek Bridge project revolutionized bridge construction by significantly reducing road closure time from six months to just 16 days, resulting in a $440,000 overall cost saving. Discover how prefabricated bridge systems are the future of infrastructure in this detailed analysis.
articles.body: The accelerated bridge construction project that replaced the U.S. 6 bridge over Keg Creek in Pottawattamie County in 2011 closed the road for 16 days instead of the roughly six months that were estimated by Iowa DOT, which would have been required with conventional construction. The bridge was completely prefabricated off-site, which made the project a demonstration of accelerated bridge construction techniques that were developed through the federal Strategic Highway Research Program. It was the first project of its kind in Iowa and was described by the Federal Highway Administration as a first in the United States for completely prefabricating the new bridge system off-site and installing it at the crossing.Most of the bridge was prepared away from trafficThe Keg Creek replacement was designed around prefabricated bridge elements rather than building the entire structure piece by piece over the existing roadway. The project used prefabricated substructure and superstructure systems, along with several other construction technologies. The bridge used high-performance and ultra-high-performance concrete, and self-consolidating concrete for parts of the foundation work. A fully contained flooded granular backfill system was installed behind the abutments.The approach meant that a lot of the work could be completed before the main road closure began, and Iowa DOT selected the Keg Creek site as part of a national research effort that examined ways to replace bridges faster while maintaining structural performance. The bridge itself was a three-span steel and precast modular structure that measured about 210 feet long and 47 feet wide. The Iowa DOT says that the bridge was chosen because its three-span configuration was common in Iowa and other states, and engineers wanted the demonstration to help figure out certain construction methods that could be applied to similar bridges elsewhere.The road closed for 16 daysIowa DOT estimated that the bridge replacement would have required a road closure and detour lasting about six months with conventional cast-in-place construction. The accelerated approach reduced the critical closure period to 14 days, although the completed replacement took 16 days from the time traffic was diverted until it returned to the road. Iowa DOT later described the bridge as a national demonstration of prefabricated bridge elements and systems, and during the project, large bridge components were prepared and assembled away from the final crossing, then brought to the site for installation. That compressed the work that had to take place directly on U.S. 6, with the shorter closure also reducing the time that commercial traffic spent on the detour.The prefabricated approach nearly doubled the initial bridge construction cost when compared with the conventional alternative. The as-built project cost about $2.66 million, in comparison with an estimated $1.51 million for the baseline construction scenario. The difference came when the analysis included costs imposed on road users.The economics changed when driver costs were includedAn FHWA economic analysis calculated vehicle operating and delay costs that were associated with the two construction approaches, and under the conventional scenario, the longer closure would have generated much higher user costs. The analysis estimated about $1.6 million in user-cost savings from the shorter construction period, and after those savings were included alongside the higher agency construction cost, the accelerated project came out about $440,000, or 29%, below the conventional alternative. The $440,000 figure was not just money that was saved on construction materials or the bridge contract, since the project cost more to build directly. The overall saving appeared after the analysis counted the economic cost of keeping motorists and commercial vehicles on a longer detour.According to FHWA's 2013 account of the project, the prefabricated bridge cost more to construct, but the shorter closure reduced vehicle operating and delay costs to a level that was enough to produce an overall advantage of about $440,000. Researchers studied the prefabricated components and the ultra-high-performance concrete connections that were used in the bridge, and testing examined the performance of the joints under laboratory and field conditions.The project became one of Iowa DOT's early examples of accelerated bridge construction and was later followed by additional bridge projects that used prefabricated elements and related techniques. The bridge itself cost more than a conventional structure, but the road was closed for only 16 days instead of months, and once the cost of traffic disruption was included, the faster construction method produced the $440,000 overall advantage.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1962, South Africa built road sections from Kalahari sand instead of crushed rock; 55 years and 1.5 million truck-equivalent loads later, all remained in service without reported structural problems
articles.summary: Discover how South Africa's innovative use of Kalahari sand has led to the construction of durable roads, enduring more than 55 years under heavy traffic without failure. Learn about the experimental techniques that revolutionized road building in arid regions.
articles.body: Southern African road builders have long struggled with an uncomfortable issue. The wide Kalahari region lacks the crushed rock and high-quality gravel typically used for road bases, and hauling those materials hundreds of kilometres can consume a large share of the project's budget. The region has an abundant supply of fine, pale sand, often dismissed as too loose to carry heavy traffic. In 1962, engineers in South Africa's Free State province tested that belief on a real road. After more than six decades, the experiment remains a strong argument for using the land's own resources.The trial is located on the R700 between Hoopstad and Bultfontein. Several experimental base sections were built using a fine-grained, Kalahari-type sand. Some sections were treated with cement, lignosulfonate, tar or bitumen, while one section was left as plain sand. Control sections alongside them used graded crushed stone, the customary choice. In his final report, AFCAP researcher F. Netterberg wrote that by June 2017, 55 years after the road opened, all sections were still carrying traffic. None had been rehabilitated, and none appeared ever to have shown a structural failure.Why sand was worth testingThe sand near Hoopstad is a Kalahari-type sand and aeolian, meaning it was deposited by wind over thousands of years. It also isn't plastic, so it doesn't act like clay and get sticky or soft when it gets wet. That made it a logical contender, but no one in 1962 could say how it would behave after years of trucks, sun and rain.That is why the experiment was designed the way it was. Cement, tar, bitumen and lignosulfonate, a by-product of the paper industry, were all tested as stabilisers to see whether they could help the sand perform better. But the most revealing section was the plainest. A 90-metre stretch of untreated sand was used as the base course with nothing added to it at all. It was there to answer a direct question: could sand alone do the job? Its performance was then compared with that of the adjacent cement-stabilised and crushed-stone sections.What the traffic showedRoad engineers measure wear in standard axle loads, which convert the mix of vehicles, including buses and large lorries, into an equivalent number of passes by a single reference axle. By June 2017, Netterberg's report said, the road had carried some 1.5 million standard axle loads per lane, and every section was still in service. The record has limits: traffic and performance data from the early decades are patchy.Further trials pointed the same way. Researchers compared untreated fine red sand, sand stabilised with bitumen emulsion, and standard gravel on Botswana's Serowe-to-Orapa road, which was built in 1989. After 19 years, two reseals and no patching, all the sand and gravel sections were in excellent to very good condition.When sand-based roads make senseThat is not to suggest motorways should be built across dunes. Traffic on the Hoopstad and Orapa roads is light, and the researchers say the findings apply to low-volume, sealed roads. They also attached conditions. The surface seal must be wide enough to accommodate the traffic, and building and surfacing must be done with great care since sand is unforgiving of shortcuts.Other work in the region supports cautious optimism. On Botswana's Kanye-to-Jwaneng route, a separate experiment followed sand, asphalt and calcrete bases for 13 years and found both base types viable for at least 1.0 million standard axle loads, despite construction flaws in some sections.A sealed, all-weather road made mainly of local sand can cost far less than one built with imported stone. The Hoopstad experiment suggests such roads can also last for generations, using material found beside the carriageway. It is a good argument for checking the ground at hand before ordering gravel from far away.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump admin sued over plan to deploy election monitors at US midterm polling stations
articles.summary: The Trump administration has been sued over its plan to deploy a large number of election monitors at polling stations across the US during next month’s
articles.body: The Trump administration has been sued over its plan to deploy a large number of election monitors at polling stations across the US during next month’s midterm elections, with the NAACP alleging that the move could intimidate voters and interfere with the electoral process.The Guardian reported that the NAACP has filed a lawsuit against Harmeet Dhillon, head of the justice department’s civil rights division, over the planned deployment. Dhillon has said she hopes to send around 1,000 monitors to polling sites during the November midterm elections.The lawsuit seeks to force the Trump administration to release records related to the planned deployment. The NAACP said it had requested the documents under the Freedom of Information Act on September 1, but the Justice Department had not complied with the request.The civil rights organisation said the release of the records was necessary to protect voting rights and ensure transparency ahead of the elections.“There is no federal statute that gives the US Department of Justice the right to send their so-called ‘election monitors’ to polling sites across the country,” said Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel and a former head of the Justice Department’s civil rights division under President Joe Biden.Clarke accused the Trump administration of seeking to disrupt how elections are conducted and said the deployment could interfere with voters’ ability to participate without intimidation.Attorney General Todd Blanche said Sunday that election monitors would be deployed in all 50 states. Speaking to Fox News, he defended the programme, saying the Justice Department had monitored elections for decades.“Since the 60s, the Department of Justice has monitored elections,” Blanche said, adding that the Trump administration was following the practice of previous administrations.The Justice Department said its election monitors would comply with all legal and ethical requirements and would not interfere with the voting process. It said the programme was consistent with its longstanding practice of monitoring elections for compliance with federal law.The deployment has also drawn criticism from within the Republican Party. Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon objected in August to the conduct of two federal election monitors who arrived at a polling station during the state's primary elections without prior notice and attempted to examine voting machines.The Justice Department rejected Gordon’s characterization of the monitors’ conduct as aggressive or improper, saying its officials had held a cordial meeting with the governor and other state officials.The NAACP, however, said monitors deployed during the primary season had arrived without public or jurisdictional notice and without clear evidence that they were present for a legitimate civil rights purpose.With the midterm elections only weeks away, the organisation is seeking judicial intervention to obtain records on the Justice Department’s plans and determine whether its election-monitoring efforts could undermine voters and local election officials.You use AI every day. articles.title: A quick lunch, then a Jantar Mantar march: How Rahul-led opposition once again kept police guessing
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: On Wednesday afternoon, Congress and INDIA bloc leaders were meeting for lunch at a restaurant on Janpath.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: On Wednesday afternoon, Congress and INDIA bloc leaders were meeting for lunch at a restaurant on Janpath. Within an hour, they were boarding buses and heading towards Jantar Mantar for a protest.The demonstration quickly took a different turn when Delhi Police stopped the buses on Ashoka Road, setting off another confrontation between Congress leaders and the police.The episode was the latest example of a 'dhappa' style protest that Rahul Gandhi and the Congress have recently used.The latest episode began after Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge announced an INDIA bloc sit-in at Jantar Mantar following the lunch."Today, we will hold a sit-in protest at Jantar Mantar. Until our demands are met, we will continue to stage such protests," Kharge announced.Delhi Police stopped the buses carrying the MPs and officers, citing a Supreme Court directive, said permission for protests at Jantar Mantar had to be sought at least 10 days in advance.The confrontation soon escalated. Congress MPs climbed on top of a bus, while Amarinder Singh Raja Warring said, "This is Rahul Gandhi's 'sena,' we won't stop."Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and other women MPs lay down on the road, while Congress workers punctured the tyres of the bus carrying Rahul Gandhi.Priyanka alleged that she was manhandled, while TMC MP Mahua Moitra alleged a lathi-charge. Police eventually detained the MPs following a brief struggle.The events followed a similar sequence a day earlier, when Rahul announced that INDIA bloc MPs would march from Parliament House to the Election Commission headquarters to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.This time, too, police were prepared. Barricades, paramilitary personnel and traffic diversions were put in place. Rahul climbed a barricade and waved the national flag before the march was stopped and several leaders were detained.But the protest did not end there.As MPs were being put into buses, Priyanka boarded one and Rahul appeared ready to follow. The two then changed course and entered the nearby Akashvani Bhawan premises.They sat under a tree near Gate No. 4, where broadcasting staff gathered outside to watch. KC Venugopal, Pawan Khera, Imran Pratapgarhi and Srinivas BV joined them, while other Congress workers climbed the boundary wall and raised slogans.Congress later circulated a video of the detour with a "dhappa" caption. After nearly nine hours, police forcibly removed Rahul, Priyanka and the other protesters.Delhi Police registered an FIR over their "unauthorised" entry into the premises. Rahul subsequently used the case as part of his political messaging."I have 45 FIRs against me. My goal is to have 100. I want 100 FIRs to be registered against me. Every FIR is a medal for me," he told reporters on Wednesday.The same approach had surfaced earlier on July 21, a day after police action against students and young people protesting at Jantar Mantar over the NEET paper leak.Congress MPs had initially been asked to assemble at party president Mallikarjun Kharge's residence at 10 Rajaji Marg to wish him on his birthday. Most MPs were not told about the larger plan in advance so that police could not prepare for the protest.After both Houses of Parliament were adjourned, Rahul and Priyanka walked towards the gate of 7 Lok Kalyan Marg, the Prime Minister's residence, around 500 metres away. Kharge and other MPs followed them.The leaders tied plastic bands around their hands and demanded the resignations of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the alleged treatment of students during the march to Parliament.The government sent minister of state in the PMO Jitendra Singh and Union home secretary Govind Mohan to the spot. Jitendra Singh tried to convince Rahul to call off the protest, saying the area was not designated for demonstrations and that "It was causing significant inconvenience to the public."Rahul, Priyanka and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav were eventually removed by police and taken to Mandir Marg and Chhatrasal Stadium before being released.For Congress, the approach has also produced a dramatic visual narrative.The recent protests are centred on the demand for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation after a report said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions taken without their knowledge.The Election Commission has rejected the suggestion of a breakdown in functioning, saying disagreements are normal in a multi-member body and that decisions were taken unanimously. articles.title: Jnanendra alleges Rs 800 crore health scam in state
articles.summary: Former Karnataka minister Araga Jnanendra alleges an Rs 800 crore scam in construction workers’ health check-up drives, seeking a probe into records and agencies.
articles.body: Shivamogga: Former minister and Thirthahalli MLA Araga Jnanendra on Wednesday alleged financial irregularities exceeding Rs 800 crore under the guise of health check-up drives for construction workers.Speaking to reporters in Shivamogga, the BJP leader claimed that funds collected through labour cess over the past three and a half years were systematically misused without conducting genuine medical screenings across the state.According to Jnanendra, the labour welfare department fixed Rs 2,950 per head for testing a worker and their dependents. Work orders totalling over Rs 799 crore were issued across 81 units to eight private agencies, with each unit assigned roughly 33,500 beneficiaries at an allocated budget of Rs 9.8 crore.Official documents report that 27.1 lakh workers and dependents were screened state-wide. However, Jnanendra asserted there are no corresponding procurement records for medical kits, required HIV test kits, doctor appointments, or biomedical waste disposal clearances from the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board.In Shivamogga district alone, records show Rs 30 crore was spent to test nearly 100,000 individuals across locations. Jnanendra noted that local inquiries revealed residents and beneficiaries were completely unaware of any such health camps taking place. Noting that legislators across multiple constituencies—including his own constituency of Thirthahalli—report no visible health check-up activity over the last three years, Jnanendra called for a comprehensive investigation into the role of officials and executing agencies.“Over Rs 800 crore meant for the health of poor construction workers has been siphoned off on paper. articles.title: Househelp held for Rs 35L jewellery theft in Delhi
articles.summary: Delhi Police arrested a newly hired househelp for allegedly stealing Rs 35 lakh jewellery and foreign currency in Bharat Nagar; all stolen items recovered.
articles.body: New Delhi: A newly appointed househelp was apprehended for allegedly starting her employment journey at a house in northwest Delhi’s Bharat Nagar with a theft of jewellery worth Rs 35 lakh, currency notes from the UAE, Malaysia and Singapore, and other valuables.The burglary was reported on Sept 29, following which police received a tip-off regarding the stolen property being kept in the Rana Pratap Bagh area. Given the high-value nature of the theft, a police team was formed to apprehend the accused. While tracing the valuables, police interrogated another househelp, Vinita, who worked at a house near the spot of the theft.During interrogation, Vinita revealed crucial information regarding the whereabouts of the stolen goods, leading to the recovery of the jewellery, currency notes and an iron safe, among other items.“Leads developed through technical surveillance and field inputs determined the involvement of the accused, Jyoti (30), who had been appointed as a househelp in the complainant’s family. She emerged as the mastermind of the burglary and was arrested by police,” said DCP (northwest) Akanksha Yadav.Police said all the stolen property was recovered, and a case has been registered at Bharat Nagar police station. articles.title: Preparations for Dussehra Mahotsav begin at Gandhi Maidan
articles.summary: Patna Dussehra Mahotsav at Gandhi Maidan runs Oct 11–14, with Ramleela Oct 11–20; officials plan security, traffic, power, cleanliness, CCTV and control room.
articles.body: Patna: Elaborate security and crowd management arrangements are being made for the Dussehra Mahotsav at Gandhi Maidan, scheduled from Oct 11 to 14. A Ramleela will also be staged at the venue from Oct 11 to 20.Reviewing preparations on Wednesday, Patna divisional commissioner Rajesh Kumar directed officials to complete all arrangements within the stipulated timeframe. He said a large number of devotees and visitors were expected to attend the events and stressed that security, law and order, and public convenience should be accorded top priority.Officials have been directed to deploy adequate magistrates and police personnel and ensure robust security at the venue. Traffic management and organised parking arrangements will also be made to facilitate smooth movement of visitors.The Patna Municipal Corporation has been asked to maintain cleanliness at Gandhi Maidan and surrounding areas. Officials concerned will inspect and ensure repairing of lighting systems and adequate illumination throughout the celebrations.Officials of the Patna Electric Supply Undertaking have been directed to ensure uninterrupted power supply, while organisers have been asked to keep backup power arrangements ready. Adequate fire tenders, drinking water facilities and temporary toilets will also be provided.The venue will be equipped with barricading, designated entry and exit gates, watchtowers and CCTV cameras for crowd monitoring.
